content:
tl;dr: A proposal to change mathlib's docs#Submodule.IsLattice to: "fg + rank condition", because we need it for polyhedral geometry.

Currently in mathlib, there are two definitions of a "lattice" (in the Zn\Z^nZn sense, not the order theory sense). We have

  1. docs#IsZLattice: In a normed space EEE over a normed field KKK, a Z\ZZ-submodule L≤EL \le EL≤E is called a lattice if it is discrete (in the topological sense) and its KKK-span is EEE.
  2. docs#Submodule.IsLattice: Let KKK be a RRR-algebra and VVV a KKK-module. Then a RRR-submodule LLL of VVV is called a lattice if it is finitely generated as a RRR-module and its KKK-span is VVV.

A group of people in Berlin are currently working on formalizing polyhedral geometry (see the Polyhedral project). In particular, some of us are thinking about defining lattice polytopes with a view of eventually doing Ehrhart theory. Unfortunately, we found neither 1. nor 2. to be workable in our setting: We avoid 1. because we are trying to develop an algebraic theory of polyhedra and polytopes, that works both over the real numbers and the rational numbers as a base field. Basically, the setting is always over a general linearly ordered field K\mathbb{K}K. So we would like a definition of lattice that works in this setting. Definition 2 is algebraic in nature, but it seems to come more from an algebraic number theory point of view which doesn't quite align with how we would like to think about lattices. There are two independent points here:

  • We would like to be able to speak about non-full-rank lattices. docs#Submodule.IsLattice demands full rank.
  • With R=ZR = \ZR=Z and K=RK = \RK=R, docs#Submodule.IsLattice does not behave well: For example, Z+Z2\Z + \Z \sqrt 2Z+Z2​ is a lattice in R\RR by this definition. But it's dense in R\RR, so it should not be considered a lattice (e.g. Gordan's lemma fails here: R≥0⊆R\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \subseteq \mathbb{R}R≥0​⊆R is a rational polyhedral cone, but the monoid R≥0∩(Z+Z2)\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} ∩ (\Z + \Z \sqrt 2)R≥0​∩(Z+Z2​) is not finitely generated).

The docstring of docs#Submodule.IsLattice suggests that the intended use case for this definition is K=Frac(R)K = Frac(R)K=Frac(R) (and most theorems in that file assume this). So in some sense it's not surprising that it behaves badly for (R,K)=(Z,R)(R,K) = (\Z,ℝ)(R,K)=(Z,R). But we work over a general linearly ordered field, so both K=Q,RK = \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}K=Q,R should be allowed. A natural generalization of the setting K=Frac(R)K = Frac(R)K=Frac(R) would be: KKK a field and a RRR-algebra with R→KR \to KR→K injective. That would cover our case, but then the definition of lattice needs to be repaired to exclude examples like Z+Z2\Z + \Z \sqrt 2Z+Z2​. So we propose to call a RRR-submodule L≤VL \le VL≤V a lattice, if:

  • It is finitely generated as an RRR-module,
  • The RRR-rank of LLL equals the KKK-dimension of the KKK-span of LLL.

Basically, this drops the requirement of being full-rank (which one would need to assume separately if needed) and adds an additional axiom that excludes examples like Z+Z2\Z + \Z \sqrt{2}Z+Z2​. One can think of this axiom as an algebraic version of discreteness. If K=Frac(R)K = Frac(R)K=Frac(R), the new definition is equivalent to the old one together with spanK(L)=Vspan_K(L) = VspanK​(L)=V (one can clear denominators, so the new axiom always holds). So we think this should still cover any application of lattices the current definition was intended for, while also allowing it to be used in our setting. However, none of us are algebraic number theorists, so we'd like to ask the broader community for opinions on this.

Also, this definition of lattice isn't new, although there aren't many references that do it like this. But there is at least one paper by Viguié which defines lattices exactly like this.

Now, if R→KR \to KR→K is injective, lattices are torsion-free modules. Hence if RRR is a PID, lattices are free modules. What our proposed definition guarantees is that, if RRR PID, one can always find a RRR-basis that's also KKK-linearly independent. That's the property of lattices we need. And we always work over PIDs (most likely Z\ZZ). We never care about the non-PID case, while we do care about the K≠Frac(R)K \neq Frac(R)K=Frac(R) case. From my limited impression reading the literature, it seems some number theorists care about the non-PID case, but don't care about the K≠Frac(R)K \neq Frac(R)K=Frac(R) case. So one question here is: Does anybody care about lattices when RRR is not a PID and K≠Frac(R)K \neq Frac(R)K=Frac(R)? And what is the "correct" definition of lattices at this level of generality?

Pinging @Christian Merten @Judith Ludwig as the authors of Algebra.Module.Lattice.lean

Justus Springer said:

Does anybody care about lattices when RRR is not a PID and K≠Frac(R)K \neq Frac(R)K=Frac(R)?

Maybe yes, for example RRR is the ring of integer of some number field whose class group is not trivial, and KKK is the completion of the number field at some place.

And what is the "correct" definition of lattices at this level of generality?

I think your new definition still valid, for that even if a Dedekind domain is not PID, an ideal of it still have rank one, although sometimes it can only be generated by two elements, but these two elements must be linearly dependent; the maximal linearly independent subset can contain only one element.
